22.0.s.en: 1. The accusation that he criticizes God's actions

22.0.0.en: 1 Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said, 2 "Can a man be profitable unto God, as he that is wise may be profitable unto himself? 3 Is it any pleasure to the Almighty, that thou art righteous? or is it gain to him, that thou makest thy ways perfect? 4 Will he reprove thee for thy piety? will he enter with thee into judgment?"

22.0.1.en: Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said [1]:

22.0.2.en: "Can a man be profitable unto God,

22.1.0.en: as he that is wise may be profitable unto himself?" [2]

22.1.1.en: Previously the three friends accused Job of hypocrisy, since they could not find any sin they could lay hold of against him. They insisted that he must certainly have been a hypocrite who did evil in secret. The sign of his hypocrisy, in their view, was that the successive calamities that had befallen him were a sign of God's anger against him. Now Eliphaz sets out a series of accusations, the first of which he tried to draw out of Job's words during the dialogue by interpreting them from their own point of view. The first of these accusations is that Job complains of God's actions and criticizes them, as though he were judging God to be unjust.

22.1.2.en: In Eliphaz's view, Job's complaint about the multitude of his calamities amounts to accusing God of injustice. This is a false accusation, for Job was as far as could be from thinking in this way.

22.1.3.en: If we set aside Eliphaz's intention in accusing Job, his speech carries a true side: that God is not in need of man's righteousness and has no benefit in it, but the benefit falls upon man, who is the object of God's love, concern and care. Prudence, or wisdom, is for the building up of man, and the source of wisdom is God.

22.1.4.en: "But wisdom is profitable to direct" (Eccl 10:10). "Godliness is profitable unto all things" (1 Tim 4:8). "If thou be wise, thou shalt be wise for thyself" (Prov 9:12).

22.1.5.en: * "Can a man be compared with God, even if he has perfect knowledge?" [2] Those who sink to the depths in bringing certain accusations, since they contradict the words of truth, often repeat what is well known, lest by holding their tongue they should seem to be defeated. So Eliphaz, pressed by the words of blessed Job, uttered things known to everyone.

22.1.7.en: * The wicked man strikes himself first, indeed he strikes no one but himself, for it is said: [He alone shall bear it] (see Prov 9:12). His soul is always full of grief, and his thoughts are always tangled, whether concerning what he hears or what he says. He does everything while complaining, bringing accusations.

22.2.0.en: St. John Chrysostom "Is it any pleasure to the Almighty, that thou art righteous? or is it gain to him, that thou makest thy ways perfect?" [3]

22.2.1.en: Man, in his weakness and limitation, is unable to offer any benefit to God, the all-perfect, who increases in nothing. Can a candle benefit the sun in any way? Can a drop of water in a cup affect the ocean?

22.2.2.en: If our ways became perfect in every respect, could they benefit God? And what pleasure would that Almighty One have if we became righteous? He is the source of peace, blessedness and joy. If He tells us in our human language that He is pleased with us, this only reveals His love for us and His longing for our salvation and glory, without His benefiting in anything of His own from our righteousness and sanctification.

22.2.3.en: * "Is there any profit to God if you are righteous? Or any gain if you set your ways right?" [3] In all this we do well, working for our own good, not for the good of God. Therefore it is said by the Psalmist: [O my soul, say to the Lord: You are my God, You have no need of my goods] (Ps 16:2). He is truly our Lord, for He is also certainly the God who has no need of anyone to serve Him, but who returns the good that He receives, so that the good things that are offered do not profit Him but those who first received them, and return again to them. The Lord says at His coming for the judgment: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me" (Mt 25:40). He says this with surpassing tenderness and sympathy for His members.

22.2.5.en: * If He did not love us, why did He create us? Is He in need of us? Do we supply Him with anything? By what service? Does He need something that we offer Him? Hear what the prophet says: [I said to the Lord, You are my Lord, my good is nothing apart from You] (Ps 16:2).

22.2.6.en: * He does not need our services as masters need their servants, but our very works return to us for our own benefit. With regard to them, masters profit from the service of the servant, but with regard to our service as servants the Master does not profit by it, rather the servant enjoys the benefit, as the Psalmist says: "my good is nothing apart from You" (Ps 16:2). Tell me: what is God's profit if you are righteous, or what happens to Him if you are unjust? Is not His nature incorruptible, never to be touched by harm, higher than all suffering?

22.3.0.en: St. John Chrysostom "Will he reprove thee for thy piety? will he enter with thee into judgment?" [4]

22.3.1.en: When God rebukes us so that we may become godly, He does not do this because of any harm that has befallen Him, but as a Father who wants us to enter into fellowship with Him, so that we become a living icon of Him, and this for our own glory. He rebukes for our sake. He does not enter into judgment like one who has been wronged, but to give us an opportunity for dialogue, so that we may sense His condescending love and His care for our salvation.

22.3.2.en: * "Is it for fear of you that He rebukes you? Or enters with you into judgment?" [4] Who thinks like this unless he has lost his senses, as though the Lord reproves us out of fear or passes sentence on us out of dread? But those who do not know how to weigh their words slip without doubt into vain speech... So Eliphaz, who uttered vain words, suddenly uttered corrupt and violent words.

22.4.s.en: 2. The accusation that Job is a dangerous wicked man

22.4.0.en: "Is not thy wickedness great? and thine iniquities infinite?" [5]

22.4.1.en: From time to time the three friends hinted at their accusation of Job, but now Eliphaz felt that it was no time for hinting but for open confrontation. He directs Job to his conscience to judge himself as a man whose wickedness is great and whose iniquities have no end.

22.4.2.en: Eliphaz portrays for us his view of Job: not merely that he is a hypocrite who hides his evils and covers over his iniquities, but that he sees him as wicked, with great wickedness and iniquities without end. It is as though he were saying to him: Language fails me to depict the evil that you are; your picture is exceedingly hideous!

22.4.3.en: * "Is not your wickedness great, and your iniquities without end?" [5] Notice how from a dead heart there come forth vain words, and from vain words he goes on to a hideous lie, and his heart was inflamed so that his tongue uttered insults. This is the degradation that comes with the increase of sin: when the tongue is not restrained, it does not stop but descends continually to what is worse.

22.5.0.en: "For thou hast taken a pledge from thy brother for nought, and stripped the naked of their clothing" [6].

22.5.1.en: Eliphaz portrays Job for us in the image of a brute. He sees him as a man who knows no mercy, with not one human touch in him. He does not take things from his brother as a pledge to secure the repayment of a loan he gives him, but takes his brother himself in pledge and holds him as a lowly hostage and as a slave who loses his freedom.

22.5.2.en: In a grave and painful exaggeration Eliphaz depicts Job as stripping the naked, who have no clothes, of their clothing! That is to say, instead of giving clothes to the naked to cover them and warm them, or at least ignoring their nakedness and the dire poverty they suffer and the cold they endure, he knows how to strip clothes from those who have none!

22.5.3.en: He accused Job of having taken some persons as hostages, put them in prison and enslaved them, because they had nothing with which to pay a debt; and of having stripped them of their garments and left them naked, which both the natural law and the Law of Moses forbid (Ex 22:26; Deut 24:13).

22.5.4.en: To bring out Job's brutality to the full, he accuses him of having enslaved not (only) a stranger, which is brutal enough, but also his brother, who is a member of his household or of his own kind.

22.5.5.en: Eliphaz did not mention the names of any persons against whom Job committed this violence, and had it been true, God Himself would not have described him as upright.

22.5.6.en: * "For you have taken a pledge from your brother for nothing, and stripped the naked of their clothing" [6]. In the Holy Bible the word "pledge" (a security or earnest) is used to refer to the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and sometimes to the confession of sin. It is used for the gift of the Holy Spirit when Paul says: [and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts] (2 Cor 1:22). For we receive the earnest so that we may have the assurance of the promise that was given us. The gift of the Holy Spirit is called an earnest because our souls are strengthened by the assurance of the inner hope.

22.5.7.en: Again, by the word "pledge" is meant the confession of a sin, as it is written in the Law: [If your brother becomes a debtor to you in anything and you take a pledge from him, you shall return it to him before the going down of the sun] (see Ex 22:26). For our brother is a debtor to us when he sins against his fellow creature in a matter that is against us. For we call sins "debts" (Mt 18:32). And in the Lord's Prayer we pray every day: [Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors] (Mt 6:12).

22.5.8.en: * "And stripped the naked of their clothing" [6]... One who is naked cannot be stripped of anything, but we ask: why are they referred to as naked and then afterwards stripped? It is necessary to know that everyone who enjoys purity of mind has not the garment of deceitful dealing (with two faces), and so he is naked. And there are some among the heretics who truly have purity of heart, and who nevertheless still hold to corrupt doctrines in their teaching. These are naked in their purity and are clothed, as it were, with the teaching of men.

22.6.s.en: 4. The accusation of opposing the doing of good

22.6.0.en: "Thou hast not given water to the weary to drink, and thou hast withholden bread from the hungry" [7].

22.6.1.en: After portraying him as a brutal man who enslaves his brother and spares no effort to strip the naked of a garment they do not have, he now presents him as a man without feeling, who gives no water to the thirsty, though water is the common property of all humanity, and who, if he sees a man giving bread to the hungry, prevents him from doing the work of mercy. So he neither does good nor lets others practice good.

22.6.2.en: He described him as a man who never did good to the poor, even those who had reached hunger and thirst, and who did not give a cup of water to the thirsty, which would have cost him nothing.

22.6.3.en: * "You have not given water to the troubled, and you have withheld bread from the hungry" [7]. For the heretics themselves think that they give water to the troubled, when they offer the cup of their errors to persons who suffer under their earthly burdens.

22.6.4.en: These consider themselves not to have withheld bread from the hungry. When they are asked, they answer with pride and boldness even about things that are unseen and beyond comprehension. They present themselves as learned above all men, even when they wretchedly dare to speak about things unknown.

22.6.5.en: But the Holy Church, when she sees someone hungry for something that is not to his advantage, either holds him back with restraint, if these matters are indeed known to her, or, if they appear to be unknown, she confesses this in humility. She recovers a sense of humility by good management when she instructs each one of them through her preaching: [not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but to think soberly] (Rom 11:20)... Thus when we see the Holy Church keeping weak minds from probing deeply into the truths, it was said to blessed Job: "You have withheld bread from the hungry."

22.7.0.en: "But as for the mighty man, he had the earth; and the honourable man dwelt in it" [8].

22.7.1.en: After distorting Job's image and presenting him as a dangerous wicked man, with limitless iniquities, brutal in nature, enslaving his brother, doing no good and preventing others from practicing it, he accuses him of showing partiality, so that if a rich or great man committed an injustice, he would not ask him about his crime.

22.7.2.en: * [that thou observe these things without preferring one before another, doing nothing by partiality] (see 1 Tim 5:21). Act without partiality, with justice, among those who are on trial, and judge them yourself, so that your mind is not occupied beforehand with anyone, nor do you lean beforehand toward anyone.

22.7.3.en: St. John Chrysostom * This was said concerning the love that it is fitting for a man to show to his neighbor. Let us be occupied with these things without committing transgression, and let us do nothing by partiality or to the shame of others, but let us love the poor as servants of God, and especially visit them.

22.7.4.en: St. Clement of Rome * "Where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work. But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality" (see Jas 3:16-17). What blessedness will not be gained by the man who prays asking for this wisdom and receives it from the Lord?

22.8.s.en: 6. He insults widows and crushes orphans

22.8.0.en: "Thou hast sent widows away empty, and the arms of the fatherless have been broken" [9].

22.8.1.en: He accused him of sending the poor widows away empty from the door of his house, and, instead of helping the orphans, of crushing their arms, so that they became unable to help themselves.

22.8.2.en: This accusation is grave, for it is counted as directed against God Himself. In the Old Testament God is reckoned a judge of the widows and a father of the fatherless. Perhaps even before the Law, those who believed in God understood this, either through the natural law or through the tradition handed down through the ages. Whoever despises a widow puts himself in a difficult position with the judge of the widows and their defender, and whoever crushes the arms of orphans is as one who has directed the blows against their heavenly Father, who prides Himself on being the Father of the fatherless.

22.8.3.en: This accusation carries a symbol of what is done by the heretics who abstain from marriage as though it were uncleanness, and from partaking of foods that God created, such as meats, as though they were defiled (1 Tim 4:3), as some of the Gnostics proclaimed. For they want to destroy the sanctity of marriage and to defile God's good creation. Souls are then turned into widows who have lost their heavenly Bridegroom, our Lord Jesus, and they have taken from her the rejoicing of the wedding, the joy of the Spirit and fellowship with the Savior. On the other hand, they want to deprive souls of the heavenly food, the bread of angels, so that they become like orphans whose arms are broken and crushed, unable to practice spiritual works.

22.8.4.en: Our Christ came to bring us back from the state of widowhood and to take away our orphanhood, since He became for us the spiritual Bridegroom and the heavenly Father. But the enemy of the good works through the wicked to return us to widowhood and orphanhood!

22.9.0.en: 10 "Therefore snares are round about thee, and sudden fear troubleth thee; 11 Or darkness, that thou canst not see; and abundance of waters cover thee."

22.9.1.en: "Therefore snares are round about thee, and sudden fear troubleth thee" [10].

22.9.2.en: This is a new accusation, namely that it was fitting for Job not to complain of what had befallen him as though it were the fruit of God's injustice to him, because all the calamities that had come upon him are from the nets that Job himself set for himself by his injustice to others and his disregard of the poor, the widows and the orphans. All his troubles are the fruit of the deeds that Eliphaz supposed him to have practiced.

22.9.3.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that this accusation is directed by the heretics against the Church throughout all ages. They claim that they know the truth and enjoy it, and they mock the true believers who practice daily repentance, saying that they terrify themselves and set for themselves deadly snares.

22.9.4.en: * "Therefore snares are round about you, sudden fear overtakes you" [10]... When the heretics look at the believing people as those who are sinking in the sins of unbelief, they accuse them that snares are around them.

22.10.0.en: "Or darkness, that thou canst not see; and abundance of waters cover thee" [11].

22.10.1.en: Eliphaz ascribes blindness to Job, saying that he was in darkness before the trials came, since he set the snares around himself by his wickedness, and here he falls into them and cannot be delivered from them. The trials pour out upon him like waterfalls that overwhelm him, and there is no one to rescue him from them.

22.10.2.en: * "And you think that you have not seen darkness, and that you have not been swept down by the force of the rushing waters" [11]... Eliphaz calls trials and sorrows rushing waters, since they rush in as one company after another, like waters that rise with wave following wave.

22.11.0.en: 12 "Is not God in the height of heaven? and behold the height of the stars, how high they are! 13 And thou sayest, How doth God know? can he judge through the dark cloud? 14 Thick clouds are a covering to him, that he seeth not; and he walketh in the circuit of heaven."

22.11.1.en: "Is not God in the height of heaven?

22.11.2.en: and behold the height of the stars, how high they are!" [12]

22.11.3.en: Eliphaz enumerates false accusations against Job, of which he is innocent. This new accusation has come: that although he claims to be devout and offers sacrifices for his children, he practices practical atheism.

22.11.4.en: Eliphaz says truly that Job believes that God is in the height of heaven, higher than all the stars, but he is a practical atheist, how? Even if God exists, He does not care about human beings and is not occupied with their sins or their righteousness; human life does not occupy God's mind. Thus Job thought it permissible to commit many great evils without end, since there is no fear of God in him.

22.11.5.en: How did Eliphaz discover the atheism of righteous Job?

22.11.6.en: Although Eliphaz has no particular names with whom Job practiced injustice and ingratitude, he reckoned himself, as a man of understanding who perceives the secrets of things, to know that there is no sin for which God punishes in this way except the sin of injustice, cruelty and lack of mercy.

22.11.7.en: Perhaps in Eliphaz's opinion Job sinned because, although he practiced certain outward behaviors to assure those around him that he was a man of God, a believing leader, his works reveal what he hides in his mind, which is that he believes that God is not in the heights of heaven and that nothing is hidden from Him. Had Job known that, he would not have ascribed injustice to God, and would have established the fear of God in his heart, and would not have said that the eye of God does not see the world (Ezek 8:12), and would have been committed to working with uprightness and mercy.

22.11.8.en: "And thou sayest, How doth God know?

22.12.0.en: can he judge through the dark cloud?" [13]

22.12.1.en: Perhaps Eliphaz sees that Job realizes that God is in the heights of heaven, but instead of offering Him the reverence due Him he made light of Him, because in the heights He cannot see through the mist and does not concern Himself with what goes on among men on earth.

22.12.2.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) comments on this phrase, clarifying the following truths:

22.12.3.en: a. God is truly in the heavens, as though hidden from mankind behind the mist, which does not allow human eyes to behold Him.

22.12.4.en: b. He is wholly present personally with each one, and wholly present with the community. His being wholly present with individuals does not negate His being wholly present with all.

22.12.5.en: c. God's heavens are on high, and yet by His divine providence He cares for every man on earth.

22.12.6.en: d. God appears as though He departs from those who sin, not because He is absent from any place, for there is no place in which God is not, but He departs from the wicked who persist in their evils, that is, His grace departs from them, so that they find no divine help to support them, because He does not work without our consent. He is absent in respect of offering help to those who reject His work in them, but He is present to them in condemning them, especially on the great day of the Lord.

22.12.7.en: e. God is wholly present in the heavenly things, and wholly on earth in the lower things. His presence on earth does not mean His departing from the heavenly things.

22.12.8.en: f. God is hidden from men, in that they cannot see Him with bodily eyes, but He is visible through His surpassing divine works. He is not comprehended by ordinary sight, but He is touched through His works and His judgments.

22.12.9.en: g. God, who is not comprehended by the bodily senses, condescends so that men may perceive Him by His illuminations in our minds, but with all that we enjoy we are reckoned as unable to comprehend Him as He is.

22.12.10.en: * "Do you consider God to be in the heights of heaven, higher than the height of the stars? And you say: How does God know?" [12-13] Very many are so foolish that they cannot fear anything except what they see in a tangible way. So they do not fear God, because they cannot see Him...

22.12.11.en: He is truly almighty at all times... He is present to each one personally, present in a certain way to everyone, so that His presence is not diminished for all together.

22.12.12.en: For although He leaves persons when they sin, He is nevertheless present to those same persons for judgment, even if He is seen as though not present to support them.

22.12.13.en: So He surrounds what is outside and fills what is within... He governs the heavenly things above without neglecting the depths below. He is present in a certain way in the lower parts without departing from the heavenly.

22.12.14.en: He is hidden in a certain way with regard to His appearance, yet He remains known through His works; He is known in His work, and yet He remains impossible to comprehend by the reckonings of the one who knows Him. He is thus in a certain way present, yet He remains impossible to see. In a certain way it is impossible to see Him, yet His judgments remain witnesses to His presence. He subjects Himself that He may be perceived by us, and the ray of His perception of Himself remains clouded over. Again, when we are gripped by the darkness of ignorance, He remains shining in our mind with the rays of His splendor.

22.12.16.en: * "Give ear to my words, O Lord" (Ps 5:1). As she (the Church) calls on the Lord, who is her helper, she passes through this evil world and reaches Him. [Consider my meditation] (Ps 5:1); the Psalmist rightly shows that this cry is from within, from the chambers of the heart, reaching God without bodily utterance, because the bodily voice is heard, but the spiritual is understood. For this is the hearing of God, not with a bodily ear, but because He is present everywhere in His majesty.

22.13.0.en: St. Augustine "Thick clouds are a covering to him, that he seeth not; and he walketh in the circuit of heaven" [14].

22.13.1.en: Perhaps Eliphaz falsely ascribes to Job that he looks upon God as having hidden Himself with thick clouds so that He is not seen by men, and as walking on the circuit of heaven as one occupied with his own glory, who does not care for the earthly creation.

22.13.2.en: It is as though Eliphaz were demanding that Job turn back from the evils he used to practice in secret, supposing that those around him did not see or perceive them, and that God Himself was not concerned with them, and therefore the trials came upon him so that Job might review himself and confess his great sins and his iniquities without end. It is fitting for Job, in Eliphaz's eyes, to realize that he has become a disgrace, not because of the calamities in themselves, but because of the disgrace behind them, on earth as in the heavens.

22.14.s.en: 9. A comparison of Job's state with the ancient world

22.14.0.en: 15 "Hast thou marked the old way which wicked men have trodden? 16 Which were cut down out of time, whose foundation was overflown with a flood: 17 Which said unto God, Depart from us: and what can the Almighty do for them? 18 Yet he filled their houses with good things: but the counsel of the wicked is far from me. 19 The righteous see it, and are glad: and the innocent laugh them to scorn. 20 Whereas our substance is not cut down, but the remnant of them the fire consumeth."

22.14.1.en: "Hast thou marked the old way which wicked men have trodden?" [15].

22.14.2.en: After Eliphaz supposed that by his wisdom and experience he had opened Job's eyes to see his sins and iniquities, he now offers him warnings, lest his fate be the fate of the wicked men of old, such as those whom the Flood overwhelmed in the days of Noah. He accuses Job of walking in the same way as they, and his life will end as theirs ended.

22.14.3.en: The way that Job walks, in Eliphaz's opinion, is not a new way, but an old way, broad and well trodden, whose end is destruction.

22.14.4.en: If Eliphaz calls Job to leave the way he is walking, which many walked long ago and perished, the Lord of glory, unlike Eliphaz, did not follow the negative way, but presented Himself as the divine Way who grants sinners forgiveness through repentance and carries them to the gates of heaven, open to them and awaiting them.

22.14.5.en: Here it is fitting for us to set a contrast between Eliphaz, who destroys others, and the Lord Christ, who gives hope to the whole world. In pride and haughtiness Eliphaz claimed to be a wise man of understanding who leads Job to recognize his sins that he had hidden from men and from God, and which he tried to ignore, so that a flood of calamities and a deluge of afflictions came upon him that will not cease until he perishes completely. But the Lord Christ is the eternal Wisdom of God, who came in humility to take the hands of the wicked without wounding their feelings, carrying them in Himself and entering with them into the divine embrace, supporting the weak and granting them His Holy Spirit, the giver of love, joy, peace, goodness and self-control.

22.14.6.en: Eliphaz tried to destroy Job's soul with false accusations. But the Lord of glory Jesus bore the accusations directed against mankind, granting them fellowship with Him in the divine nature to lift up their souls, and granting them health of body, soul and spirit on an eternal level, where man is glorified in his entirety on the great day of the Lord.

22.14.7.en: * "Will you give a sign of the old way that the wicked tread?" [15] Since the way of our Redeemer is humility, the way of the world is pride. And so the wicked tread the way of the world, where by the lusts of the world they walk in self-conceit.

22.14.9.en: * If we also, beloved brethren in Christ, if we put Him on, if He is the way of our salvation, we who follow Christ in the steps of salvation, let us walk imitating Him as the Apostle John teaches us: "He that saith he abideth in him ought himself also so to walk, even as he walked" (1 Jn 2:6).

22.14.10.en: Martyr St. Cyprian * He is the house to which we go; He is the way by which we go. Let us go by Him to Him; so that we do not lose the way.

22.14.11.en: St. Augustine * Hold fast first to what they bore witness of themselves, saying: "As ye have therefore received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk ye in him" (Col 2:6)... For He is the way that leads to the Father; do not walk in the angels, for this way does not reach there.

22.14.12.en: St. John Chrysostom "Which were cut down out of time?"

22.15.0.en: "whose foundation was overflown with a flood" [16].

22.15.1.en: The Flood overtook the wicked suddenly while they were unprepared, thinking they would live many years, so they were drowned and perished as though it were before the time. The Flood hastened their lives suddenly. They had made the earth their foundation, and built their hopes upon it, and thought they were secure as upon a rock foundation, but the flood poured out upon this their foundation. [the flood upon the world of the ungodly] (2 Pet 2:5).

22.15.2.en: Some may ask: Is not the span of man's life known beforehand to God, so how is it said that the wicked are cut down before their time?

22.15.3.en: Do they die before the appointed time set for them? And do the days of the righteous' lives lengthen beyond what God appointed for them?

22.15.4.en: First: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that every man has a span of life that is fitting for him, that suits or deserves him. But God also knows beforehand that it is better for this wicked man to die early so that he does not cause the righteous to stumble, or He leaves him to a longer life to give him an opportunity that perhaps he may repent.

22.15.5.en: So what is said about a man's life being shortened or lengthened does not mean that God changes His mind about what He knew before, but that man receives a longer life or has his life shortened for a divine wisdom, whether with respect to the person himself or those around him, and He also knows beforehand what is fitting, whether to add to or subtract from a certain person's life as he needs to be according to nature or according to his deserving.

22.15.6.en: Second: Origen sees that the measures of life differ among men from what they are with God. As the Psalmist says, [One day with the Lord is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day](a). On the great day of the Lord we shall be surprised by little children who are reckoned as persons who lived many years, and by old men whom we see as little children.

22.15.7.en: To illustrate this, if we compare the unborn John the Baptist when he leaped with joy in the womb of his mother, St. Elizabeth, we find that by the human measure he had not yet been born, and the time of his stay in the womb is not counted as part of his age, whereas in God's sight and by His measures he is counted as a mature man, older than the high priest, the priests, the scribes, the Pharisees and so on at that time, because they are counted as dead men who did not bear witness to the Lord Christ in spite of their knowing the prophecies intellectually.

22.15.8.en: Righteous men may die as children and be reckoned as having lived thousands of years in the eyes of the Lord, and the days of wicked tyrants may be prolonged and their days be reckoned as nothing. [Their spirit goes forth, they return to their dust](b).

22.15.9.en: When we hear the Lord's commandment: "Honour thy father and thy mother, that thy days may be long upon the land," we are not astonished if a son or daughter dies at an early age in spite of their honoring their parents, for this son (or daughter) is reckoned as one whose life was long on earth, because one day of his life is reckoned with the Lord as a thousand years. This is the spiritual, symbolic interpretation that Origen adopted in many places when he spoke of man's life on earth.

22.15.10.en: According to this interpretation the wicked are cut down before their time because their lives are without fruit; they did not benefit from the opportunities of repentance to enjoy fellowship with God, the Giver of life. By their death they are reckoned as dead men who lost life and did not take care to enjoy it.

22.15.11.en: * "Who were taken before the time, when the flood poured out upon their foundation"... Every man is taken from this life at a time known beforehand, before the ages, by divine authority. But it is necessary to know that Almighty God, in creating us and ordering our affairs, appoints the limits (of our life) according to the deserving of each one. It may be necessary for the wicked man to live a short time, lest he harm many who walk uprightly, and it may be necessary for the good man to remain a longer time in life, so that he may be a help in good works to many.

22.15.12.en: Again, the wicked man must remain a longer time in life so that he may add evil deeds to his deeds. And so the righteous man may practice a sincere life that is purified by his trial, or it may be necessary to take the good man away more quickly, lest, if he lived longer, he might corrupt his innocence.

22.15.13.en: But let it be borne in mind that it is God's compassions that give sinners an opportunity for repentance. In any case, times may be granted to them, and they do not return to bear the fruits of repentance but serve evil, and by God's mercy they receive the times in the hope that they may abandon their ways.

22.15.14.en: Although Almighty God knows beforehand the time of death of each one, when his life ends, no one can die before his time, but at the time appointed for his death, for if fifteen years were added to Hezekiah's life (2 Kgs 20; Isa 38), then the time of his life truly increased beyond the end that he deserved, and God had already known his time at this moment and the time at which afterwards He would take him from the present life.

22.15.15.en: This is how it is: what does [the wicked are cut off before their time] mean but that all those who love the present life prepare themselves for longer periods of that life? And when death draws them out of the present life, the long periods of their life that they were accustomed to imagine are taken from them; they are cut to pieces. Rightly it was said of these: [their foundation was overflown with a flood]...

22.15.16.en: Cain is described as the first to found a city on the earth (Gen 4:17), and by this he clearly confirmed that he was a stranger, since he was a stranger to steadfastness in the eternal world, and so he laid a foundation on the earth. Being a stranger to the heavenly things, he set his stability in a foundation of lower things, and set the stability of his heart in earthly pleasure.

22.15.17.en: Just as with the collapse of daily time the state of death in the present life itself runs toward its end, and shatters the dedication of the sons of perdition by removing these very persons, rightly it was said of the wicked: [their foundation was overflown with a flood], that is, the same change casts into them the instability of the wicked's constructions.

22.15.19.en: "Which said unto God, Depart from us:

22.16.0.en: and what can the Almighty do for them?" [17]

22.16.1.en: The sin of these wicked is that they ask God: "Depart from us," since they want to live without God, so that their consciences do not rise up and they do not lose their dullness. They ignored Him, saying: "The LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil" (Zeph 1:12).

22.16.2.en: They had heard of Him that He is the Almighty, but in their eyes what authority has He over them?

22.16.3.en: As we said before, atheism is of two kinds: either denial of the existence of God, or, while knowing that He exists, they think that He does not feel for them, far from them in His heavens, or they ask Him to depart from them, since they consider Him unable to give them the happiness they seek or to fulfill for them what they desire.

22.16.4.en: "Yet he filled their houses with good things:

22.17.0.en: but the counsel of the wicked is far from me" [18].

22.17.1.en: What increases the condemnation of the wicked is that they enjoyed good things that were from the Almighty, and they misused them. Those who were drowned in the Flood [were eating and drinking, they married wives, they were given in marriage, they bought, they sold] (Lk 17:27). They had no justification for asking "What can the Almighty do for them," for they were living in His abundant good things, and they had no reason to call upon the Maker of good things to depart from them. Their houses were full of good things, but their hearts were empty of divine grace, and therefore they perished.

22.17.2.en: Here Eliphaz agrees with Job in the desire: "the counsel of the wicked is far from me" (Job 21:16).

22.17.3.en: * "But he fills the houses of the wicked with good things" [18]. The Lord fills the houses of the wicked with good things, even for the ungrateful, for He does not withhold His gifts, so that they may be ashamed of the compassion of their Creator and return to goodness, or they may despise returning, and that will be a cause of their punishment with greater severity, since they repay God's surpassing goodness with evil, and so harsh woes come upon them afterwards...

22.17.4.en: "May their judgment be far from me." This too blessed Job expressed, when he says: [let their counsel be far from me] (Job 21:16).

22.18.0.en: "The righteous see it, and are glad: and the innocent laugh them to scorn" [19]

22.18.1.en: The righteous are not to be reckoned thus, as though they were pleased with the death of the wicked and mocked them; rather they groan and pray for them. But on the Day of Judgment, when opportunities were given to the wicked and they persisted in their wickedness, turning their backs on the Giver of life and preferring sonship to the devil instead of sonship to God, then, as destruction comes upon them, which is the work of their free evil will and conduct, the righteous are glad, since there is no longer any place for evil in them, but they live in the heavenly holy Jerusalem with the holy God.

22.18.2.en: The righteous do not gloat over the wicked at their perdition, for they carry the will of their Father that all be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth, but they rejoice at the annihilation of the authority of evil and injustice so that the weak may not stumble, as they are glad at the glory of God, which does not admit corruption.

22.18.3.en: The righteous find the opportunity to reveal the futility, weakness and transience of evil, and the foolishness of the wisdom, cunning and malice of the wicked. The righteous are glad at the collapse of the devil and his kingdom, and at the destruction of sin, not of the sinner. For the righteous man knows nothing but love, even toward sinners.

22.18.4.en: * "The righteous see it and rejoice, and the innocent laugh them to scorn" [19]. When the righteous see the wicked sinning here, they do not rejoice at the fault of people who destroy themselves. For if they rejoiced at the fault they would no longer be reckoned righteous... The Pharisee lost his righteousness because he was pleased, reckoning himself higher than the tax collector, saying: [I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican](c).

22.18.5.en: Again, if we say that the righteous man can triumph with complete joy over the death of the wicked, what kind of joy is this for the sake of vengeance on the wicked in this world, in which the life of the righteous is not secure?

22.18.6.en: Let us distinguish between the times of terror and those of glory. The righteous see the wicked now and become wasted because of their evils. And when they see them being smitten, they do not trust in their own lives either... Now the righteous see the sons of perdition and groan, and at the final judgment they will see them and laugh in derision.

22.19.0.en: "Were not our adversaries destroyed, and the fire has consumed their remnant?" [20]

22.19.1.en: Perhaps he refers here to Lot, who tormented his righteous soul with the lawlessness of the wicked, for though he lost everything he possessed, he desired the salvation of the people of Sodom and Gomorrah as he rejoiced at the destruction of corruption and lawlessness (2 Pet 2:7-8).

22.19.2.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that those who oppose the righteous and are hostile to the divine truth will be cast into the fire of Gehenna that is not quenched, which burns souls with bodies. Just as the body shared with the soul in opposing God and they cooperated together in practicing the works of the devil and submitting to him, so it is fitting that they share the devil's fate, the eternal fire.

22.19.3.en: * Although the wicked depart from here from their dead body, they receive it again in the resurrection, so that in the same body they burn, the same body with which they committed sin. Since their sin was in the mind and the body, so the punishment will be in the spirit and the body alike.

22.19.5.en: The righteous believer rejoices when he sees the opponents of the divine truth, that is, the evil thoughts that want to creep inside and gain control over the inner man. Such evil thoughts are burned by the fire of the Holy Spirit, as thorns are burned by fire. So everything that is foreign to the pure nature that God created in us is burned, to kindle the fire of divine love.

22.19.6.en: The believer rejoices in the fiery work of the Holy Spirit in him, who destroys and builds!

22.20.s.en: 10. Repentance is getting acquainted with God

22.20.0.en: "Acquaint now thyself with him, and be at peace:

22.20.1.en: thereby good shall come unto thee" [21].

22.20.2.en: It is difficult to judge this attitude of Eliphaz, for although he wronged Job by directing bitter accusations against him, and tried to confirm them in spite of his inability to find practical proofs of his accusations, here he opens before him the door of hope.

22.20.3.en: Eliphaz reveals the blessings of returning to God by repentance. If we set aside Eliphaz's intention to confirm Job's wickedness, his words here are a strong source of hope in returning to the Almighty, so that he may find in the Almighty Himself his good, his righteousness, his treasure and all his satisfaction.

22.20.4.en: Eliphaz offers good counsel: [Draw near to God, get acquainted with Him, and be at peace with Him!] There is no remedy but drawing near to God, uniting with Him and entering with Him into inner peace.

22.20.5.en: * There is none who grieves us like the one who has fallen into sin, who remembers his sins to take pleasure in earthly fleshly things, instead of his mind being occupied with the beautiful ways of knowing God!

22.20.6.en: For Adam hid himself when he learned of God's presence, wishing to hide when God called him, with that matter by which he wounded his soul (not meeting the Lord), saying to him: "Adam...: Where art thou?" (Gen 3:9). That is, "Where are you hiding yourself? Why do you conceal yourself? Why do you flee from God, whom you longed to see?!

22.20.7.en: St. Ambrose "And be at peace": that is, be at peace with God, or with yourself, where you find rest in Him, for evil is a source of inner anxiety.

22.20.8.en: What is the "good" that Eliphaz looks to as a fruit of entering into peace with God? If he means the heavenly blessings, his counsel is sincere and constructive, but if his eyes are fixed on the temporal goods that Job lost, then he has not been right in his counsel!

22.20.9.en: * "We have peace with God" (Rom 5:1), through our Lord Jesus Christ, who reconciled us with God through the sacrifice of His blood...

22.20.10.en: Christ came to destroy the enemies, to make peace, and to reconcile us with God, from whom the barrier of evil that we erected by our sins had separated us.

22.21.s.en: 11. Repentance is a personal enjoyment of the Word

22.21.0.en: "Receive, I pray thee, the law from his mouth, and lay up his words in thy heart" [22].

22.21.1.en: He who enters into peace with God finds the divine commandment sweet, issuing as though from His divine mouth directly into his heart, and in sweetness and delight man cries out: "Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?" (Acts 9:6).
